blocks.text: In the book On Falcons, Goshawks and Hawks, Chapter 3, at the end of the Remains of Frederick II on the Art of Hunting with Birds, edited by Joh. Gottl. Schneider, p. 180; his Commentaries, p. 187–189, should also be compared.

The Syriac Physiologus, edited by Tychsen, Chapter 15, also renders the Hebrew אנפה as charadrius, ܟܪܐܕܪܝܘܣ. He describes the bird as entirely white, with no blackness in it at all (ܐܝܬܝܗ ܚܘܪܬܐ ܟܠܗ ܘܠܝܬ ܒܗ ܐܘܟܡܘܬܐ ܡܕܡ). "But among all the charadrii listed by Linnaeus, Hasselquist, Forsskål and Buffon (says Tychsen in his Commentary on this Chapter, §. 2, p. 91), not a single one is found that is entirely white and could be reconciled with our author's charadrius. Moreover, nothing is found in this migratory bird for which it should be thought especially worthy of the company of princes."

To me, however, Tychsen's conjecture seems closer to the truth: that the Arabs rendered the Hebrew אנפה as parrot, ببغا [bbghā], either because the Greek translators took χαραδριον [charadrion] to be a parrot, or because they sought help from the etymology. "For אנף means to breathe, to be angry, to snort with anger; and the parrot is not only by nature the most prone to anger of all birds, but when an unknown person approaches it, it usually snorts very fiercely, whether from anger, from aversion, or from fear."
Book 1, ch. 20, p. 136 etc., and book 2, ch. 16, p. 242.

There can be no doubt that this bird is the Oriolus Galbula of Linnaeus (T. 1, vol. 1, p. 383, 13th ed.), or the picus nidum suspendens [woodpecker that suspends its nest] of Aldrovandi, Ornithol. vol. 1, book 12, p. 854 ff., which seems to be the same as Pliny's galgulus; his words in book 10, ch. 33 are: they affirm that the galguli themselves sleep hanging by their feet, because they hope they are safer that way. I shall add some passages from Aldrovandi to confirm and illustrate what Bochart has adduced from the Arabs. As I was eager, he says, to observe the skill which the bird is said to use in building its nest, behold, Cesare Rinaldi, a patrician of Bologna, opportunely sent me as a gift a nest found on his estate. This nest imitated a little bowl exactly: round, that is, and hollow, made entirely of hemp fibres, and attached at the top to a branch of a walnut tree already laden with fruit. To one who merely looks at it, its skill is not really apparent; but to one who examines it, nothing more ingenious seems possible to be made by a bird devoid of reason. For, wishing to build a nest of this kind, namely round and hollow, it had to search through many trees for a branch suitable for giving it that hemispherical shape; and being able to find one only in part, it chose among others this forked branch, because one of its forks, ending as it were in an elbow, came closer than the others to roundness. Nor does the whole skill depend on this, since it is far greater in the fastening of the hemp to the branches. For it is wound around them so ingeniously that you would think it made not by a bird but by men. But not even this will seem wonderful, if you hear what I am now going to say and examine closely how the whole hollow of the nest, hanging downward in the air, can support four young, and fairly large ones, indeed larger than adult sparrows, when, as I said, it consists entirely of prepared hemp, and that quite limp: so, lest this mishap should occur, the bird provided in this way: it strengthened the nest on the outside so excellently with certain thicker and stronger threads that it could be equal to a far heavier weight.
